title: Head‑to‑head Evaluation of Translation‑First vs Agentic Generate→Validate→Repair Pipelines for Intent‑Driven NetOps Changes — Validator‑Acceptance Parity under Shared‑Candidate Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑archived paired experiment (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) that compared two operational architectures for intent→configuration NetOps changes across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and Mininet‑derived topologies: (A) translation‑first (constrained vendor DSL → formal verifier → solver) and (B) agentic generate→validate→repair (hosted LLM + deterministic validators). The run declared gpt‑5‑mini for generation and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 for deterministic end‑to‑end correctness checks; preregistration used shared_initial_candidate semantics so each task pair received a single LLM candidate shared between arms. Execution completed 240 episodes (120 paired tasks) with model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair). Deterministic scoring produced contingency counts n11 = 120, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (baseline = 120/120; guarded = 120/120). Paired difference (A − B) = 0.00; paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Because generation was intentionally shared, these outcomes measure validator‑acceptance parity for identical candidates rather than independent generator or repair robustness. The preregistered hypotheses H1 and H2 about comparative generator/repair performance were therefore preregistered but unobserved under the shared_initial_candidate execution; we explicitly report the artifact evidence supporting that restriction (preregistration id, provider call audit, and per‑task scoring traces) and provide concrete instructions and resource counts required to exercise the original H1/H2 in follow‑ups.

sections.introduction: Automating intent→CLI translation and safe sequencing of multi‑vendor NetOps changes is operationally critical: production networks require correctness guarantees (reachability, isolation, absence of transient safety violations) while supporting diverse intents across vendor CLIs. Two canonical architectures are: (A) translation‑first pipelines that restrict generation to a vendor DSL and apply formal verification/solvers, and (B) agentic generate→validate→repair pipelines that centralize generation in an LLM and rely on deterministic validators plus bounded repair loops. We preregistered a paired experiment (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) to compare these two approaches on a common set of intent tasks (N=120 paired tasks), with a single primary estimand: the paired difference in binary end‑to‑end operational correctness (A − B). The preregistration fixed generator = gpt‑5‑mini, validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5, and an orchestration choice we call shared_initial_candidate: each paired task received the same single LLM candidate, generated once and supplied identically to both arms. That design intentionally removes generator variance so the measured estimand is validator‑acceptance parity for identical textual candidates. Importantly, the preregistered hypotheses H1 (translation‑first yields higher correctness rate) and H2 (agentic pipeline achieves greater repair coverage but more transient unsafe proposals) concern comparative generator and repair performance under independent sampling; because our execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics these hypotheses were preregistered but are unobserved in this run. This manuscript reports the artifact‑grounded outcomes for the measured estimand, documents why repairs were never invoked in the execution artifacts, and points to the specific preregistration and execution changes required to test H1/H2 in future runs.
sections.related_work: Two research strands frame our design choices. Formal translation→verification systems (e.g., SymNet, related verification frameworks and Weighted NetKAT variants) emphasize constrained output spaces and solver‑backed determinism, enabling binary accept/reject validator semantics and counterexample traces useful for proof and repair [10, 11, 5]. LLM‑driven NetOps and AIOps work emphasizes flexible natural‑language→CLI mapping, sample‑based generation, and iterative repair instrumentation; such studies commonly allocate larger model‑call budgets, instrument multi‑sample diagnostics, and measure repair coverage and transient unsafe‑proposal rates [3,4]. Prior comparisons vary on whether they (i) hold generator outputs fixed between arms (validator‑parity semantics) or (ii) sample independently per arm (generator/repair semantics). Our preregistration deliberately chose the former (shared candidate) to answer an operational question relevant to validator/orchestrator swaps: will downstream acceptance change when the same candidate is evaluated by different orchestration/verification stacks? This run sits adjacent to, but does not replace, independent‑sampling comparisons required to evaluate generator robustness or repair efficacy.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and execution contract. The study preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1) fixed: paired design with 120 confirmatory task pairs, generator = gpt‑5‑mini, deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (v5.0), execution adapter = hosted_netops_gvr_v1, and shared_initial_candidate semantics. The analysis executor was paired_binary_analysis_v1 (bootstrap percentile 95% CI, exact McNemar test). The preregistration, its SHA‑256, and planned analysis details are archived in the execution manifest.

Task generation and orchestration. Confirmatory tasks were produced deterministically (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) and each manifest entry contains intent text, canonical reference answer, initial/expected final states, and required safe sequences; representative manifest entries are archived (execution/task_manifest.jsonl). The orchestration implemented shared_initial_candidate: for each task pair a single LLM generation was produced and provided identically to both downstream arms. Provider audit evidence (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json and execution/execution_manifest.json) records hosted_model_call_event_count = 120 and model_calls_used = 120, consistent with one shared call per pair.

Provider‑call contamination checks. To rule out inadvertent leakage of canonical reference answers into model prompts, provider_call traces were archived for each shared generation. Representative provider_call artifacts (for example, execution/provider_calls/task-000001-shared-initial.json) show the prompt composition used for the model: system/instruction role + task intent and constraints (intent text and allowed fields/workflow policies derived from the task manifest). The canonical reference_answer is stored separately in the task manifest (execution/task_manifest.jsonl) and is not included in the prompt payloads archived in the provider_call files; the provider_call artifacts therefore show prompts that do not contain the canonical reference answer. The execution manifest and provider audit confirm no cross‑condition cache reuse or prompt‑state leakage (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json: cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false).

Validator scoring and repair instrumentation. deterministic_netops_validator_v5 applies full_intent_constraint_validation: syntactic normalization, required command inclusion, ordering/dependency checks (e.g., make‑before‑break, shutdown→modify→restore), final state consistency, and outputs validation_after.valid (boolean) and repair_applied (boolean). Per‑task scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/task‑000XXX‑*.json) record parsed_command_count, required_command_count, normalized_response, validation_before/after snapshots, repair_applied flags, and repair_provider_trace_path (when repairs occur). These per‑task files are the canonical evidence for whether the validator accepted a candidate and whether repairs were invoked.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The execution manifest reports planned_episode_count = 240 (120 pairs × 2 conditions), completed_episode_count = 240, failed_episode_count = 0, and model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair). Provider audit (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json) reports hosted_model_call_event_count = 120, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 120, failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 0, cache_miss_count = 120, cache_hit_count = 0, and cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false.

Primary contingency and statistical summaries. The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 120, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0, yielding marginal success rates baseline = 120/120 = 1.0 and guarded = 120/120 = 1.0. The paired difference (A − B) = 0.00. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729; analysis/analysis_log.jsonl) = [0.00, 0.00]. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. These results are deterministic given the degenerate contingency.

Why repair was never invoked. Every archived per‑task scoring JSON shows repair_applied = false and repair_provider_trace_path = null (examples: execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json, execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json). Representative validator traces show parsed_command_count == required_command_count and validation_after.valid == true (e.g., execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json: parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4, repair_applied = false). Because the shared candidates satisfied the validator's syntactic and dependency checks, the repair subsystem—though present in the orchestration and enabled by the preregistration (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1)—was not triggered. The absence of repairs is thus an observed artifact in execution/scoring/*.json rather than a post‑hoc omission; analysis/condition_summary.csv and analysis/missingness_summary.csv summarize repair_applied = 0 across all episodes.

Contamination and missingness diagnostics. Contamination checks produced no flags (analysis/contamination_summary.csv empty). Missingness diagnostics report complete_pairs = 120 and zero for any missing or failed episodes (analysis/missingness_summary.csv). Provider audit confirms execution isolation and absence of prompt reuse across conditions.
sections.discussion:
What the run measures and what remains unobserved. By design (shared_initial_candidate) this run answers a restricted operational question: given identical textual LLM candidates, do the translation‑first and agentic orchestration/verification stacks produce different deterministic validator acceptance outcomes? The artifactized answer is: no — both stacks accepted all 120 shared candidates (n11 = 120). This validator‑acceptance parity does not address generator variance, repair coverage, or differences that would arise under independent sampling. Accordingly, the preregistered hypotheses H1 and H2 (concerning comparative generator/repair performance) were preregistered but remain unobserved here; the preregistration and analysis artifacts make that restriction explicit (see CAND‑2026‑001‑prereg‑v1 and analysis/results.json).

Evidence supporting lack of contamination and live repair subsystem. The provider_call artifacts (example: execution/provider_calls/task-000001-shared-initial.json) show prompts composed of system instructions, the task intent, and allowed/forbidden constraints derived from the task manifest; the canonical reference_answer is stored only in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and is not present in provider_call payloads. Per‑task scoring traces (e.g., execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json) show parsed_command_count == required_command_count and repair_applied = false, demonstrating that candidates satisfied the validator and that the repair path—though present and instrumented by design—was not exercised. These concrete artifact references are archived in the execution bundle and constitute the primary evidence for the contamination‑free, repair‑absent outcome.

How to obtain a discriminating comparison for H1/H2. To test the original H1/H2 one must modify the preregistration to (i) generate independent LLM candidates per arm (remove shared_initial_candidate) which increases initial model_calls_used from 120 to 240, (ii) optionally sample multiple initial candidates per arm to estimate generator variance (further increasing model_call budget), and (iii) enable and instrument repair iterations so repair_applied counts and repair_provider_trace paths become nonzero and measurable. Each change produces distinct, archived signatures (hosted_model_call_event_count > 120, nonzero repair_applied in execution/scoring/*.json) that will support confirmatory tests of the preregistered hypotheses. The preregistration already documents these resource implications and how the analysis executor must be adapted.

Threats to validity. Internal validity is preserved for the measured estimand because shared_candidate eliminated generator variance intentionally; construct validity is limited because the binary validator compresses graded correctness into a pass/fail gate (however, per‑task parsed_command_count and violation_codes archived in execution/scoring/*.json permit graded follow‑up analyses); external validity is limited by emulator use (Mininet‑derived topologies), a single model (gpt‑5‑mini) and a single validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). All these limitations are explicitly recorded in the preregistration and the manuscript's limitation list.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, artifactized paired experiment comparing translation‑first and agentic generate→validate→repair pipelines under shared_initial_candidate semantics. For 120 paired tasks deterministic validators accepted identical LLM candidates in both arms for every pair (n11 = 120), yielding paired difference 0.00 (bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.00], McNemar p = 1.0). No repairs were applied (repair_applied = false in all per‑task traces); hence preregistered hypotheses about comparative generator/repair performance remained unobserved in this execution. The run provides reproducible, per‑task validator traces and provider_call artifacts that (i) rule out prompt contamination of canonical references and (ii) show the repair subsystem was live but not triggered. We release the full artifact bundle and document the precise preregistration modifications and resource counts required to exercise the original H1/H2 in a discriminating follow‑up.

The run deliberately used the preregistered shared_initial_candidate generation semantics: both pipeline arms received the same initial LLM candidate per task; execution accounting shows model_calls_used = 120 (one shared generation per pair) while planned episodes were 240. Provider_call artifacts (for example, execution/provider_calls/task-000001-shared-initial.json) show prompts composed of system instructions, the task intent, and constraints derived from the task manifest; canonical reference answers are stored separately in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and are not included in provider_call prompts (no prompt→reference leakage). limitations: Preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics were used; this intentionally removes generator variance and prevents this run from assessing independent generation robustness differences between architectures.

The task corpus was synthetic and executed in an emulator (Mininet‑derived topologies and public vendor example grammars); emulator‑to‑hardware divergence limits external validity to production devices.
A single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) were used; results do not imply multi‑model or multi‑validator generality.
No repairs were applied in this run (repair_applied = false in per‑task traces); preregistered secondary estimands about repair coverage remain unobserved for this execution.

The binary deterministic validator acceptance metric does not capture operator‑facing properties such as explanation quality, maintainability, or human trust, which matter in production but were outside the metric used here.
